And it was narrated from Ibn 'Abbas that it is the stars of the constellation Capricorn (al-Jady). Perhaps that star was well known among the Arabs, and it became famous for the Pleiades.

It has also been said that *al-tariq* means a kind of meteor, because the meteor shoots down and appears as if it runs across the sky, just as a traveler moves when the night overtakes him. So the definiteness in the word "the star" is for comprehensiveness (*al-istighraq*), and its generality is specified by its being a predicate of the pronoun referring to the one who knocks. That is, the meteor, when it falls, is seen moving swiftly and then disappears from view, appearing as if it had come to rest. It resembles the quick movement of a traveler at night to reach inhabited places, and when he reaches them, his journey stops.

The answer to the oath is His saying: ﴿Indeed, over every soul there is a guardian﴾. It is made a figurative allusive metonymy (*kinaya talwihiyya ramziyya*) for the intended meaning, which is the affirmation of the Resurrection. So it is like the evidence for its establishment, for the appointment of a guardian requires something that he guards, namely the deeds, good and bad, and that requires the intention of reckoning for them and recompense according to what they require, a deferred recompense after the life of this world, so that the deeds of the doers are not left in vain (*sudan*). That requires that the recompense be deferred until after this life, since it is observed that recompense often fails to occur in this life. So if recompense were neglected, its neglect would contradict the wisdom of the All-Wise God who originated this universe, as He said: ﴿Did you think that We created you in vain?﴾ [al-Mu'minun: 115]. And this deferred recompense requires the return of life to the selves from which the deeds proceeded.

These are four implications, by which the metonymy became allusive and figurative.

Along with this inference there results the information that over the souls there are guardians, so this is *idmaj* (incorporation, the embedding of one meaning within another).

The *hafiz* (guardian) is one who keeps a matter and does not neglect it, so that a desired purpose results from it.

The majority of readers recited *lamma* with a light *mim*, while Ibn 'Amir, Hamzah, Abu Ja'far, and Khalaf recited it with a doubled *mim*.

According to the reading with a light *mim*, *in* is the light form of the heavy *in* (*in mukhaffafa min al-thaqila*), and *lamma* is composed of the *lam* that distinguishes the negative *in* from the light form of the heavy *in*, together with the superfluous *ma* after the *lam* for emphasis. According to the reading with a doubled *mim*, *in* is negative and *lamma* is a particle meaning "except" (*illa*), for *lamma* is used with the meaning of *illa* in negation and in oaths. You say: "I asked you *lamma* you did such-and-such," i.e., "except that you did such-and-such," on the estimate: "I ask you only for doing such-and-such," so it returns to negation. Each of the light *in* and the negative *in* is preceded by the oath.

This answer contains, in addition to affirming the reckoning, a warning to the polytheists that God knows their beliefs and their deeds, and that He will requite them for that.

He elaborated in describing this gushing fluid in order to incorporate instruction and admonition regarding the subtle details of formation, so that the ignorant disbeliever may awaken and the believer may increase in knowledge and certainty.

"Khuruj" (emergence) is used for the beginning of movement from one place to another, even without coming into view, for the emergence of this fluid does not occur from between the backbone and the ribs as an outward appearance.

The "sulb" is the bony column located in the middle of the back, which is the spinal column with its vertebrae.

This is an address to people in terms of what they knew at that time in a general statement, together with an alert that the creation of man from the fluid of the man and the fluid of the woman is indicated by the mention of the taraʼib, because the most well-known view is that it is applied only to the area between the woman's breasts.

There is no doubt that offspring is formed from the man and the woman. It forms from the man's fluid, which contains small bodies called in medicine the spermatozoa (al-hayawanat al-manawiyyah), which are elongated threads composed of a flattened oval-shaped head and a thin tail like a thread. From these threads the fertilization of the offspring occurs in the woman's womb. Their seat is the two testes (al-unthayan), which are the two glands that produce the semen, and it then propels into the woman's womb.

And from a fluid that belongs to the woman, like the semen to the man, called the woman's fluid, which consists of minute ova of round shape found in a liquid whose seat is a follicle among the follicles contained in the woman's two ovaries. These are equivalent to the man's testes; they are two glands located on the two sides of the woman's womb. Each ovary contains a number of follicles ranging from ten to twenty. The egg's emergence from the follicle occurs at the completion of the follicle's maturation. When its maturation is complete, it bursts and the egg emerges into a canal that carries it to the cavity of the womb. The egg's maturation and its emergence from the follicle are completed at the time of the woman's menstruation, so conception greatly increases when a man has intercourse with a woman near the end of her menstruation.

In the man, the two vessels connect with the spinal cord, which is the backbone, and then end at a vessel called the seminal cord (al-hablu al-manawi), composed of arteries, veins and nerves, and it ends at the two testes, which are the two glands that secrete the semen. There it forms in a fatty manner and remains dispersed in the two testes until the two testes secrete a fatty, greasy substance, and that occurs upon the stimulation and friction of the penis, which is connected to the two testes, and it gushes into the woman's womb.

As for the woman, the two vessels behind the ears pass over the upper chest of the woman, which is the taraʼib, because the two breasts are located there, and they are among the organs connected to the vessels through which the menstrual blood flows, carrying the ova from which offspring come. Menstrual blood flows from the openings of vessels in the womb, which are vessels that open when the time of menstruation arrives and contract after purification, and a nerve reaches the womb from the brain.

This is among the scientific miracles of the Qur'an, of which there was no knowledge among those to whom it was first revealed. It is a general indication, and the Hadith of Muslim clarifies it, narrated from Umm Salamah and 'A'ishah: "The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) was asked about a woman's wet dream, and he said: 'She must perform ghusl when she sees the fluid.' It was said to him: 'Does a woman see that?' He said: 'And does resemblance arise except from that? When the woman's fluid overcomes the man's fluid, the child resembles his maternal uncles, and when the man's fluid overcomes hers, the child resembles his paternal uncles.'"

The fa' (فَ) here indicates that the command to give respite follows from the whole preceding discourse, from His words ﴿Indeed, it is a decisive word﴾ [al-Tariq: 13], with its explicit statements, allusions, clarifications, and promise of victory. The meaning is: do not hasten on their behalf by asking for the punishment to descend, for it will certainly befall them.

At-tamhil (التَّمْهِيلُ) is the verbal noun of mahala, meaning amhala, which is giving respite, granting a delay either to a specified time or to an unspecified one. The combination of mahhil and amhilhum is therefore a repetition for emphasis, intended to increase the sense of calm. The two verbs differ in their transitive form: one is doubled (with tashdid) and the other uses the hamza, in order to make the repetition more elegant.

The intended meaning of al-kafirin (الكافِرِينَ) is those referred to by the pronoun in ﴿Indeed, they are plotting a plot﴾ [al-Tariq: 15]. It is therefore an explicit noun in place of a pronoun, to condemn them by the blame of disbelief. The intended meaning is not all disbelievers but specifically the known disbelievers.

Ruwaydan (رُوَيْدًا) is the diminutive of rawd, with a damma on the ra' and a waw after it. It may be an ism al-masdar (verbal noun). As for the regular verbal noun of its root, it is rawd, with a fatha on the ra' and sukun on the waw, meaning delay and absence of haste. It is an emphatic verbal noun for the verb amhilhum, so it has emphasized His words ﴿So give respite to the disbelievers﴾ twice.

The meaning is: wait for what will befall them, and do not hasten on their behalf in the manner of one who waits with hostility and deliberation. Thus ruwaydan is a kinaya (allusive metaphor) for the certainty of the punishment that will befall them, because one who is confident that something will occur does not hasten it.

Its diminutive form indicates a reduction in quantity, meaning: a respite that is not long.

It is also permissible that ruwaydan here be an ism al-fi'l (verb-substitute noun) in the sense of an imperative, as in the expression ruwaydaka (رُوَيْدَكَ). The attachment of the second-person kaf to it is not a condition when it is used as an ism al-fi'l. In that case, the pause would be after al-kafirin, and ruwaydan would be an independent statement. The existence of a verb with the same meaning before it is not evidence that it is used as a verbal noun. The meaning would then be: be patient and do not hasten the descent of the punishment upon them. It is therefore a kinaya for the promise that it will certainly occur.

Surah al-A'la (سُورَةُ الأعْلى)

This surah is reported in the Sunnah under the name "Surat (Glorify the name of your Lord, the Most High)". In the two Sahihs, on the authority of Jabir ibn 'Abdullah, who said: "Mu'adh stood and led the late night prayer ('isha'), and he prolonged it. Some of those who prayed behind him complained about him to the Prophet ﷺ. The Prophet ﷺ said: 'Are you causing trouble, O Mu'adh? Where were you from [reciting] "Glorify the name of your Lord, the Most High" and "By the morning brightness"?'" End of quotation.

In Sahih al-Bukhari, on the authority of al-Bara' ibn 'Azib, who said: "The Messenger of God ﷺ did not come to Medina until I had recited 'Glorify the name of your Lord, the Most High'" among surahs similar to it.

Al-Tirmidhi related on the authority of al-Nu'man ibn Bashir that "the Messenger of God ﷺ used to recite 'Glorify the name of your Lord, the Most High' and 'Has there come to you the report of the Overwhelming?' in the 'Eid prayer and on Friday."

'A'isha named it "(Glorify)". Abu Dawud and al-Tirmidhi related from her: "The Prophet used to recite in the witr prayer, in the first rak'a, '(Glorify...)'" and so on. This is apparent in that she intended the naming, because she did not give the complete Qur'anic phrase. Likewise al-Baydawi and Ibn Kathir named it that, because it is distinguished by opening with the word "Glorify" in the imperative form.

Most exegetes and scribes of the Mushafs named it "Surat al-A'la", because the attribute al-A'la (the Most High) occurs in it and not in any other surah.

It is Meccan according to the majority, and the hadith of al-Bara' ibn 'Azib that we mentioned just now indicates this. However, it is reported from Ibn 'Umar and Ibn 'Abbas that His words, the Exalted, ﴿He has succeeded who purifies himself and remembers the name of his Lord and prays﴾ [al-A'la: 14], were revealed concerning the 'Eid prayer and the zakat al-fitr. That is, these two are Medinan, so the surah would be partly Meccan and partly Medinan.

It is reported from al-Dahhak that the whole surah is Medinan.

[Page 272]

The meanings it contains bear witness that it is Meccan. It is enough to cite His words, the Exalted, ﴿We will make you recite, so you will not forget﴾ [al-A'la: 6].

In the order of the revelation of the surahs, according to Jabir ibn Zayd, it is counted eighth. It was revealed after Surat al-Takwir and before Surat al-Layl. It is reported from Ibn 'Abbas, 'Ikrima, and al-Hasan that it is seventh. They said: "The first thing revealed of the Qur'an was 'Read in the name of your Lord', then Nun, then al-Muzzammil, then Tabbat, then 'When the sun is wrapped up', then 'Glorify the name of your Lord.'" As for Jabir ibn Zayd, he counted al-Fatiha after al-Muddaththir, and then counted the rest, so it is eighth in his reckoning. It is therefore among the early surahs, and His words, the Exalted, ﴿We will make you recite, so you will not forget﴾ [al-A'la: 6] call out to that.

The number of its verses is nineteen, by the agreement of those who count verses.

* * *

It includes the glorification of God, the Exalted, and an allusion to His oneness, by His sole creation of man and His creation of what is on the earth of what sustains its existence.

It includes the support and strengthening of the Prophet ﷺ in receiving the revelation.

It also includes that God will give him an easy law and a Book by which those with pure souls, who fear their Lord, will be reminded, while those of wretchedness who prefer the worldly life and do not care for the eternal life will turn away.

And that what has been revealed to him is confirmed by what is in the books of the messengers before him. All of this is a lightening of what he encounters of the aversion of the polytheists.
